summary:
SPHEREx Web Explorer is an open-source web tool that lets anyone inspect how the infrared sky changes between SPHEREx survey passes. Enter an object name or coordinates and the app fetches cutouts live from NASA's IRSA archive, subtracts the zodiacal background, masks flagged pixels, aligns the exposures north-up and blinks the epochs for each detector, the way volunteers used WiseView to find brown dwarfs.

Beyond blinking, the app detects and tracks sources across epochs, fits proper motions, compares them with Gaia DR3 and CatWISE2020, and ranks them with an explainable anomaly score. A shift-and-stack search looks for movers too faint to see in single epochs, and a spectro-temporal view shows each source's flux by wavelength and time. Volunteers can classify what they see.

On real data the tool measures the motions of Barnard's Star and Epsilon Indi B in agreement with Gaia, recovers the cold brown dwarf WISE 0855, and detects the fading of RW Aurigae. Results are candidates for human inspection, not discovery claims.
details:
SPHEREx Web Explorer — a web tool for finding moving and variable objects in SPHEREx data

WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months in the infrared (0.75–5 µm). SPHEREx Web Explorer lets anyone compare those passes at any sky position. The user types an object name or coordinates; the app resolves the position (SIMBAD, including proper motion), finds every SPHEREx exposure there through NASA's IRSA archive, and downloads small cutouts in parallel. Each exposure has its zodiacal background subtracted and its flagged pixels masked, is resampled onto a common north-up grid, and is combined per survey epoch and per detector. Frames are streamed to the browser as soon as they are ready and can be blinked, differenced or averaged, with adjustable contrast, zoom, a sky-coordinate readout and a crosshair that follows the target's proper motion.

On top of the viewer, the app analyses the field automatically:

- detects and tracks sources across epochs and fits their proper motions;

- measures aperture photometry in mJy with uncertainties, and refuses saturated or masked apertures instead of inventing values;

- compares every source with Gaia DR3 and CatWISE2020 at the observation epoch;

- ranks sources with an explainable anomaly score (motion, variability, missing catalogue counterpart) and lists the reasons for each rank;

- runs an optional shift-and-stack search for movers too faint to see in a single epoch, checked against time-shuffled control searches;

- shows a spectro-temporal view, F(λ, t): the flux of each exposure at its own wavelength and time, as spectra by epoch, light curves per detector and change statistics compared with reference stars in the same field;

- lets volunteers classify sources, stores the votes, and exports results as JSON or CSV.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

WiseView let volunteers discover nearby brown dwarfs by blinking WISE images. SPHEREx adds 102 colours and repeated all-sky coverage, but had no comparable public tool. SPHEREx Web Explorer is meant to give citizen scientists and students that tool: a way to search for fast-moving nearby objects, cold brown dwarfs and a possible distant planet, and to notice variable stars, with nothing to install. Every automatic result is presented as a candidate for human inspection, with its uncertainties and reasons for caution, never as a discovery claim.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES AND SOFTWARE

Backend: Python with FastAPI and Uvicorn; Astropy, Astroquery, PyVO, NumPy, SciPy and Photutils for astronomy and image processing; SQLite for volunteer classifications. Frontend: plain JavaScript, HTML and CSS using the Canvas API, with IndexedDB caching in the browser and no framework or build step. Data: SPHEREx images from the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), Gaia DR3, CatWISE2020 and SIMBAD. Testing and delivery: pytest (137 automated tests, including tests on real SPHEREx cutouts), Git and GitHub, with a Docker setup included. No special hardware was needed. AI coding assistants (Claude) were used for parts of the code, interface and documentation; results were checked against real data and automated tests.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

The sky fills the whole screen and the controls are movable, resizable windows that appear only when needed, in the style of a game menu, so the data stays in front. The tool combines a visual blink comparator with automated discovery, an explainable ranking, and a shift-and-stack search with built-in controls, all in a browser. It treats a SPHEREx spectrum as what it really is: measurements taken at different wavelengths and at different times.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Scientific honesty: statistical errors plus measured systematic floors; limits stated openly (3–4 epochs per field, so motions are good to about 0.4–1 arcsec per year).

- Wavelength: detectors are never mixed in one image series, because they see different colours.

- Validation on real targets: the measured motions of Barnard's Star and Epsilon Indi B agree with Gaia within the uncertainties; WISE 0855 is recovered by shift-and-stack; RW Aurigae's fading is detected; R Draconis is reported as saturated rather than measured.

- Archive reliability: retries, time limits, a Stop button and local caching for when IRSA is slow or unavailable.

- Future data: SPHEREx data releases are discovered at run time, not hard-coded.
